In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HBV reactivation in lymphoproliferative disorders is a rare event.
HBV reactivation can occur in lymphoma patients who are HBsAg‐negative and anti‐HBc‐positive, with or without anti‐HBe antibodies and/or anti‐HBs antibodies.
HBV reactivation in lymphomas with HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive is common, and can be fatal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chemotherapy‐induced hepatitis in lymphoma patients who have resolved HBV infection is not uncommon and can be managed with close monitoring of viral load and prompt antivirals.
HBV reactivation can occur in patients with resolved HB infection, and it can be managed with entecavir therapy.
chemotherapy‐induced hepatitis in patients with resolved HBsAg infection is not rare.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HBV reactivation in lymphomas is not uncommon and is not always predictable.

lymphoma patients who have resolved HBV infection should be carefully monitored for HBV reactivation during and after chemotherapy, and should be given prompt antiviral treatment when HBV reactivation occurs.

chemotherapy‐induced hepatitis reactivation in lymphoid malignancy patients with “resolved hepatitis B virus (Hepatitis B) infection” is not uncommon and is associated with a high risk of hepatitis flares.
